title: cafaye — every error in the fleet
description: The answer to 'one place to see all errors for the whole system' (PLAN.md §7b). Read the header below before editing a query: the predicate is span STATUS, and error.type is a drill-down inside a service. A fleet-wide breakdown grouped by error.type is the documented mistake.

panels.title: Is the system healthy right now
Error ratio (fleet, last 5m)
panels.description: THE PREDICATE IS SPAN STATUS. otel.status_code="ERROR" over all calls, per service. Not grouped by error_type: the semconv expects high cardinality in error.type when no filter is applied, and a global breakdown by it is invalid however good it looks.

panels.title: p95 request duration
panels.description: From the spanmetrics duration histogram. Core's metrics schema allows http.route and the status CLASS as dimensions, never the raw 500-valued status code, and never a tenant or user id — those are on the resource, which is exempt from the 2000-combination cap.

panels.title: Services reporting
panels.description: A fully-down service has an error ratio of nothing, because it is not serving. Silence is its own signal — see the 'A service has exported no spans' alert rule.

panels.title: Errors, by service (the predicate is span status)
Error rate by service
panels.description: Partitioned by service.name, filtered on status_code = STATUS_CODE_ERROR. §7b's answer, in one query: which service is failing, over time.

panels.title: Error class, inside one service
panels.description: THE DRILL-DOWN, AND ONLY UNDER A SERVICE FILTER. error_type is a bounded snake_case class from core's vocabulary; §7b and the semconv both say consumers expect HIGH CARDINALITY in it when no filter is applied, so it is never a fleet-wide grouping key. The service filter is the ${service} template variable, which is what makes this panel legal.

panels.title: Error log records (the crash layer)
panels.description: Every container's stderr, with no per-language SDK: §7b's second error layer, obtained for free because all six languages already write fatal errors to stderr. The collector drops exception.message and exception.stacktrace — the attributes that would carry a stack trace, and on muse a path straight to a prompt — so a record here is a class, not a transcript.

panels.title: Error spans, straight from Tempo
panels.description: Tempo's own documented error workflow: {status=error} and only then break it down. A span that reached Error with no error.type is still an error and still shows up here, which is precisely why status is the predicate and error.type is not.

options.content:
**The predicate for "this is an error" is span status `Error`, not `error.type`.**

`error.type` is a *classification beneath* that predicate. Tempo's own documented error workflow filters `{status=error}` and only then breaks the result down, and the OpenTelemetry semantic conventions say consumers should expect *high* cardinality in `error.type` when no filter is applied. So:

- **partition by `resource.service.name`** — that is `by (service_name)` on every panel above;
- **filter on status = error** — `otel.status_code="ERROR"` here, `{status=error}` in Tempo;
- **use `error.type` only as a drill-down inside a service** — the table above is scoped to the `${service}` variable, and that scoping is what makes it legal rather than wrong.

A span that ended in Error but carried no `error.type` still appears on the traces panel and still counts in the error rate. A dashboard that groups fleet-wide by `error.type` would show a different, less useful total, which is the specific failure PLAN.md §7b calls out by name.

`tests/validate.sh` asserts all three properties on this file's JSON: that no panel groups by an error class without a service filter, that at least one panel filters on status, and that at least one partitions by service. A "fix" that makes that check go red is a dashboard that answers the wrong question.
